Patience of God
PAY-shuns of GOD
noun phrase (theology proper / divine attributes)
The divine attribute (also called longsuffering or forbearance) by which God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance. Grounded in the divine self-revelation (Exodus 34:6, longsuffering), 2 Peter 3:9 (longsuffering... not willing that any should perish), and Romans 2:4 (the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering).

See also: Patience of God

Biblical Definition

The divine attribute (also called longsuffering or forbearance) by which God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance. God's patience is an aspect of His goodness directed toward the guilty: as mercy is His goodness toward the miserable and grace is His goodness toward the undeserving, so patience (longsuffering) is His goodness toward the guilty, expressed in His withholding of the judgment they deserve and His granting of time and opportunity for repentance. The biblical foundation: (1) the divine self-revelation, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth (Exodus 34:6); (2) Romans 2:4, Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?; (3) 2 Peter 3:9, The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance; (4) 1 Peter 3:20, the longsuffering of God waiting in the days of Noah; (5) Romans 9:22, God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction. God's patience is displayed throughout redemptive history: His longsuffering with the antediluvian world (1 Peter 3:20), with Israel's repeated rebellions (Nehemiah 9:17, 30-31, thou art a God ready to pardon... slow to anger, and of great kindness), and with sinners in every age. The patience of God is not indifference to sin or weakness in judgment; it is the deliberate withholding of deserved judgment to give space for repentance, and it has limits — the patience of God, despised and presumed upon, gives way to judgment when the appointed time comes (Genesis 6:3; Romans 2:5, the treasuring up of wrath against the day of wrath). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's patience against the presumption that abuses it (treating God's delay of judgment as license for continued sin, 2 Peter 3:3-9; Ecclesiastes 8:11) and the impatience that despairs of it (failing to recognize the longsuffering goodness of God that leads to repentance, Romans 2:4). God is patient — longsuffering, forbearing, slow to anger — bearing with sinners and giving space for repentance; His patience is a substantive expression of His goodness, leading sinners to repentance, and is not to be presumed upon or despised.

Webster 1828 Definition

The divine attribute (longsuffering, forbearance) by which God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance; Exodus 34:6 (longsuffering), Romans 2:4 (the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance), 2 Peter 3:9 (not willing that any should perish); not to be presumed upon.

PATIENCE OF GOD, n. phr. (theology proper / divine attributes; also longsuffering, forbearance) God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance. An aspect of His goodness toward the guilty. Foundation: Exodus 34:6 (longsuffering, and abundant in goodness); Romans 2:4 (the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance); 2 Peter 3:9 (longsuffering... not willing that any should perish); 1 Peter 3:20 (longsuffering in Noah's day); Romans 9:22. Not indifference to sin nor weakness in judgment, but the deliberate withholding of judgment to give space for repentance; it has limits (Genesis 6:3; Romans 2:5). Not to be presumed upon (2 Peter 3:3-9) nor despaired of.

Key Scripture

Romans 2:4 — "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?"

2 Peter 3:9 — "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Exodus 34:6 — "And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."

Nehemiah 9:17 — "But thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not."

Modern Corruption

The patience of God is His longsuffering withholding of deserved judgment to give space for repentance; the corruptions are the presumption that abuses it (license for sin) and the impatience that despairs of it; God's patience is not indifference to sin and has limits.

expand to see more

The patience of God is held against two errors. The presumption that abuses God's patience treats His delay of judgment as license for continued sin: because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11); the scoffers presume upon God's longsuffering, mocking the delay of judgment (2 Peter 3:3-4). This contradicts the biblical teaching that God's patience is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), not to embolden sin, and that the abuse of God's patience treasures up wrath against the day of wrath (Romans 2:5). The impatience that despairs of God's patience fails to recognize the longsuffering goodness of God, supposing that God's delay of judgment means He does not see or care; this contradicts the biblical teaching that God's apparent slowness is His longsuffering, not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is patient — longsuffering, forbearing, slow to anger — bearing with sinners and giving space for repentance; His patience is a substantive expression of His goodness, designed to lead sinners to repentance (Romans 2:4); but His patience is not indifference to sin nor weakness in judgment, and it has limits — the patience of God, despised and presumed upon, gives way to judgment when the appointed time comes (Genesis 6:3; the flood; the patience that waited in Noah's day eventually gave way to the deluge). The believer responds to God's patience with repentance and gratitude, neither presuming upon it as license for sin nor despairing of it in the face of delayed judgment, but recognizing the longsuffering goodness of God that leads to repentance and extends the day of salvation.

Hebrew Roots

Exodus 34:6; Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9; 1 Peter 3:20; Nehemiah 9:17; God longsuffering, withholding deserved judgment to give space for repentance; not to be presumed upon; has limits.
